title: Correction: the grove bed is standing on a bridge over nothing
question: Do you want the test bed's floor put on solid ground? It would make every past grove measurement non-comparable with every future one, which is why I am asking rather than doing it.
context_md:
This corrects the two cards I posted an hour ago (20260905T180757522Z-168b0f and 20260905T181311503Z-098fac). Both are still open and BOTH ARE FRAMED WRONG -- I told you the ground loss was root-bound soil holding a slope that bare soil loses. It is not. Please read this before judging those.

The picture is a bare grove bed -- no plants at all -- at frames 6,000 / 12,000 / 18,000 / 24,000. Soil band, a thin grey stone floor, and then pure black void all the way to the bottom of the world. That is the actual scene: PlantScene puts its floor 512 wide and 6 thick over 80 empty rows, anchored only at the two world edges, because the code reads off-world as bedrock.

Stone's max_unsupported_span is 16, which gives the load model a capacity base of 128 against a 3,072-cell section spanning 512 cells. That slab CANNOT pass. It stands anyway because nothing ever disturbs it: over these 24,000 frames the run reports zero overloaded failures, zero unsupported failures, and 0 of 40 chunks awake. A tree falling on it is what wakes it, and then it goes.

Roots still come out ahead and I am not walking that back: with them on, the same seed runs to 36,000 frames carrying 33 fallen log pieces (1,568 cells) with zero overloads and the floor intact -- more fallen mass over twice the time than the arm that collapsed. What I cannot tell you on one seed is WHY, because its biggest single log was 526 cells and 44 rows tall against 619 and 74.

Filed as open-bugs-handoff.md §W3. The practical cost today: any plant number taken on a grove run past ~15,000 frames may have been measured over collapsing terrain.
